techniques.name: Attribute Removal (Fairness Through Unawareness)
techniques.description: Attribute removal, also called fairness through unawareness, trains and runs a model without the protected attributes, such as race, gender or age, among its inputs. This meets the unawareness criterion, under which an algorithm counts as fair so long as it does not explicitly use a protected attribute, and it rules out direct discrimination on those attributes. It does not make outcomes fair. Other features can act as proxies, meaning they correlate with a removed attribute and let the model reconstruct it, for example a postcode standing in for ethnicity. For that reason the technique is best seen as the simplest baseline, to be combined with methods that look at outcomes.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment agency's data team builds a CV-ranking model for graduate roles and leaves gender, ethnicity and age out of its inputs, so that shortlisting cannot use them directly. It records that education institution and postcode may still carry some of that information and treats this as an open risk, to be handled with other methods.

A bank's credit-risk team removes sex and ethnicity from the inputs to a loan-approval model so that its decisions cannot use them directly, as its lending policy requires. It keeps the two fields in a separate monitoring table, so approval rates can still be compared across groups after launch.

A health-system analytics team builds a postpartum depression risk model from insurance claims and first tries leaving race out of the inputs. It then measures disparate impact between Black and White patients and compares the result with other bias-reduction methods on the same data, to decide whether removal is enough.

limitations.description: Proxy features keep the removed attribute's influence in the model. Postcode, school or employment history can predict race, sex or age closely enough for the model to reproduce group differences without seeing the attribute. In a published comparison on Medicaid postpartum depression data, removing race left disparate impact at about 0.6 (1 is parity), less effective than the other methods compared.

Proxies cannot be found by inspecting the feature list, because group membership can be spread across many features, and checking outcomes by group needs the very attributes that were removed. A team that deletes the column outright loses the ability to see whether the problem remains.

Removal alone is weak compliance evidence. Regulators that test for disparate impact or indirect discrimination look at outcomes, not inputs, so a model that never saw the attribute can still fail the test.

Removal can hurt the group it is meant to protect. Where the link between features and outcomes differs by group, dropping the attribute can raise error for the group concerned. Kusner et al. give a case where an 'unaware' predictor perpetuates unfairness, and Dwork et al. note that errors can come from ignoring group membership.

resources.title: Fairness Through Awareness
resources.abstract: We study fairness in classification, where individuals are classified, e.g., admitted to a university, and the goal is to prevent discrimination against individuals based on their membership in some group, while maintaining utility for the classifier (the university). The main conceptual contribution of this paper is a framework for fair classification comprising (1) a (hypothetical) task-specific metric for determining the degree to which individuals are similar with respect to the classification task at hand; (2) an algorithm for maximizing utility subject to the fairness constraint, that similar individuals are treated similarly. We also present an adaptation of our approach to achieve the complementary goal of "fair affirmative action," which guarantees statistical parity (i.e., the demographics of the set of individuals receiving any classification are the same as the demographics of the underlying population), while treating similar individuals as similarly as possible. Finally, we discuss the relationship of fairness to privacy: when fairness implies privacy, and how tools developed in the context of differential privacy may be applied to fairness.

resources.title: Counterfactual Fairness
resources.abstract: Machine learning can impact people with legal or ethical consequences when it is used to automate decisions in areas such as insurance, lending, hiring, and predictive policing. In many of these scenarios, previous decisions have been made that are unfairly biased against certain subpopulations, for example those of a particular race, gender, or sexual orientation. Since this past data may be biased, machine learning predictors must account for this to avoid perpetuating or creating discriminatory practices. In this paper, we develop a framework for modeling fairness using tools from causal inference. Our definition of counterfactual fairness captures the intuition that a decision is fair towards an individual if it the same in (a) the actual world and (b) a counterfactual world where the individual belonged to a different demographic group. We demonstrate our framework on a real-world problem of fair prediction of success in law school.

resources.title: Comparison of Methods to Reduce Bias From Clinical Prediction Models of Postpartum Depression
resources.abstract: Importance: The lack of standards in methods to reduce bias for clinical algorithms presents various challenges in providing reliable predictions and in addressing health disparities. Objective: To evaluate approaches for reducing bias in machine learning models using a real-world clinical scenario. Design, Setting, and Participants: Health data for this cohort study were obtained from the IBM MarketScan Medicaid Database. Eligibility criteria were as follows: (1) Female individuals aged 12 to 55 years with a live birth record identified by delivery-related codes from January 1, 2014, through December 31, 2018; (2) greater than 80% enrollment through pregnancy to 60 days post partum; and (3) evidence of coverage for depression screening and mental health services. Statistical analysis was performed in 2020. Exposures: Binarized race (Black individuals and White individuals). Main Outcomes and Measures: Machine learning models (logistic regression [LR], random forest, and extreme gradient boosting) were trained for 2 binary outcomes: postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum mental health service utilization. Risk-adjusted generalized linear models were used for each outcome to assess potential disparity in the cohort associated with binarized race (Black or White). Methods for reducing bias, including reweighing, Prejudice Remover, and removing race from the models, were examined by analyzing changes in fairness metrics compared with the base models. Baseline characteristics of female individuals at the top-predicted risk decile were compared for systematic differences. Fairness metrics of disparate impact (DI, 1 indicates fairness) and equal opportunity difference (EOD, 0 indicates fairness). Results: Among 573 634 female individuals initially examined for this study, 314 903 were White (54.9%), 217 899 were Black (38.0%), and the mean (SD) age was 26.1 (5.5) years. The risk-adjusted odds ratio comparing White participants with Black participants was 2.06 (95% CI, 2.02-2.10) for clinically recognized PPD and 1.37 (95% CI, 1.33-1.40) for postpartum mental health service utilization. Taking the LR model for PPD prediction as an example, reweighing reduced bias as measured by improved DI and EOD metrics from 0.31 and -0.19 to 0.79 and 0.02, respectively. Removing race from the models had inferior performance for reducing bias compared with the other methods (PPD: DI = 0.61; EOD = -0.05; mental health service utilization: DI = 0.63; EOD = -0.04). Conclusions and Relevance: Clinical prediction models trained on potentially biased data may produce unfair outcomes on the basis of the chosen metrics. This study's results suggest that the performance varied depending on the model, outcome label, and method for reducing bias. This approach toward evaluating algorithmic bias can be used as an example for the growing number of researchers who wish to examine and address bias in their data and models.

techniques.name: Fair Adversarial Networks
techniques.description: Fair Adversarial Networks is a pre-processing method, proposed by Cevora (2020), that rewrites a dataset so that a protected characteristic such as race, sex or age is hard to predict from it, including through proxies such as postcode or occupation. It trains two neural networks against each other. An autoencoder (a network that learns to reproduce its input) rewrites each record while staying as close to the original as it can, and an adversary network tries to predict the protected characteristic from the rewritten records. The autoencoder is penalised both for changing the data and for the adversary's success, so over alternating rounds of training it strips out the information the adversary relies on and changes little else. The output is the rewritten dataset, which any downstream analysis or model can use unchanged, and in the paper success means a freshly trained adversary does no better than always guessing the most common category.

example_use_cases.description: A probation service's analytics team wants to model reoffending from defendant records in which race is encoded indirectly, through charge descriptions and neighbourhood. It runs the records through a Fair Adversarial Network before modelling and confirms that a freshly trained classifier predicts race from the transformed data no better than always guessing the most common group.

An HR analytics team at a courier company building an absenteeism model removes information about employees' age group from its personnel records, including through proxies such as length of service and family circumstances, so that the standard modelling tools its analysts already use can run on the transformed data unchanged.

A local education authority allocating support funding with a model of school performance data de-biases the data with respect to each school's majority ethnic composition before modelling, and keeps the adversary's chance-level result and the reconstruction error with the funding model's documentation as evidence of what was removed and how much the data changed.

limitations.description: No public implementation is known. The paper withholds the parts that make training practical (an approximation of how well a fully trained adversary would do, a stabilising mechanism and regularisers) as its company's intellectual property, saying only that standard approaches can replicate the result on a one-off basis with heavy tuning, and the company's web tool is no longer online. Adopting the method means reimplementing it from the paper.

It removes every detectable relationship with the protected characteristic, including relationships that are legitimate or deliberately protective; the author notes it also removes positive discrimination. Where the characteristic carries legitimate information, such as sex in some clinical data, that information goes along with the bias, and the accuracy drops seen on the demonstration datasets cannot be split into bias removed and signal lost.

Success is judged against one adversary: in the paper, a single-hidden-layer network trained from three random starts. A more capable model may still recover the characteristic, and the author states that residual discrimination is likely still present, so a chance-level adversary is weaker evidence than it appears. The paper reports no downstream accuracy or fairness results; the only application evidence is the same company's Rosa demonstration.

Every variable in every record can be altered by the autoencoder, so the de-biased dataset no longer contains the original values. Individual records cannot be checked against source data, feature meanings drift, and any explanation of a downstream model refers to transformed features rather than to the applicant's actual postcode or income.

Adversarial training is unstable and its settings have no principled choice: the weight balancing reconstruction against the adversary, the network architectures and the stopping point all need tuning per dataset. The paper keeps the lowest-loss state to guard against run-away training and describes its own convergence as fairly sub-optimal.

resources.title: Fair Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: The influence of human judgement is ubiquitous in datasets used across the analytics industry, yet humans are known to be sub-optimal decision makers prone to various biases. Analysing biased datasets then leads to biased outcomes of the analysis. Bias by protected characteristics (e.g. race) is of particular interest as it may not only make the output of analytical process sub-optimal, but also illegal. Countering the bias by constraining the analytical outcomes to be fair is problematic because A) fairness lacks a universally accepted definition, while at the same time some definitions are mutually exclusive, and B) the use of optimisation constraints ensuring fairness is incompatible with most analytical pipelines. Both problems are solved by methods which remove bias from the data and returning an altered dataset. This approach aims to not only remove the actual bias variable (e.g. race), but also alter all proxy variables (e.g. postcode) so the bias variable is not detectable from the rest of the data. The advantage of using this approach is that the definition of fairness as a lack of detectable bias in the data (as opposed to the output of analysis) is universal and therefore solves problem (A). Furthermore, as the data is altered to remove bias the problem (B) disappears because the analytical pipelines can remain unchanged. This approach has been adopted by several technical solutions. None of them, however, seems to be satisfactory in terms of ability to remove multivariate, non-linear and non-binary biases. Therefore, in this paper I propose the concept of Fair Adversarial Networks as an easy-to-implement general method for removing bias from data. This paper demonstrates that Fair Adversarial Networks achieve this aim.

resources.title: Demonstrating Rosa: the fairness solution for any Data Analytic pipeline
resources.abstract: Most datasets of interest to the analytics industry are impacted by various forms of human bias. The outcomes of Data Analytics [DA] or Machine Learning [ML] on such data are therefore prone to replicating the bias. As a result, a large number of biased decision-making systems based on DA/ML have recently attracted attention. In this paper we introduce Rosa, a free, web-based tool to easily de-bias datasets with respect to a chosen characteristic. Rosa is based on the principles of Fair Adversarial Networks, developed by illumr Ltd., and can therefore remove interactive, non-linear, and non-binary bias. Rosa is stand-alone pre-processing step / API, meaning it can be used easily with any DA/ML pipeline. We test the efficacy of Rosa in removing bias from data-driven decision making systems by performing standard DA tasks on five real-world datasets, selected for their relevance to current DA problems, and also their high potential for bias. We use simple ML models to model a characteristic of analytical interest, and compare the level of bias in the model output both with and without Rosa as a pre-processing step. We find that in all cases there is a substantial decrease in bias of the data-driven decision making systems when the data is pre-processed with Rosa.

sample_claims.text: A classifier trained on the de-biased reoffending dataset cannot predict defendants' race better than always guessing the majority group.

The personnel records used to train the absenteeism model were rewritten so that a freshly trained classifier predicts employees' age group, including through proxies such as length of service, no better than always guessing the most common group.

The school funding data stayed close to the original after de-biasing, with the reconstruction error recorded and judged acceptable by the analysts, while the adversary's accuracy at predicting majority ethnic composition fell to chance.

techniques.name: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
techniques.description: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations (LAFTR) trains an encoder that turns each record into a representation, a vector of learned features, from which a protected attribute is hard to recover, so that models later built on that representation by other parties, including for prediction tasks not known in advance, also treat groups fairly. It was designed for a data owner who shares encoded data with downstream model builders and cannot control how they train. During training, the encoder, a decoder that reconstructs the input and a classifier for the original task play against an adversary network that tries to predict the protected attribute from the representation; the encoder is updated to defeat the adversary while keeping the information the other two need. The adversary's objective is matched to demographic parity, equalised odds or equal opportunity, and the authors prove that an optimal adversary's objective bounds that unfairness measure for any classifier trained on the representation (for the two error-rate measures the adversary also sees the labels used in training, so the attribute is hidden given the label, and the bound is with respect to those labels). The output is a frozen encoder, delivered with the accuracy and fairness of classifiers trained on top of it.

example_use_cases.description: A data marketplace that supplies customer records to advertisers wants assurance that the targeting models advertisers build will not show offers to men and women at different rates. It trains LAFTR with the demographic parity adversary, releases only the encoded features, and audits a sample of advertisers' models for the gap in positive rates and for how well a fresh classifier can recover gender from the released features.

A health insurer's data team shares encoded claims and prescription data with external analytics suppliers who build their own risk models. It trains LAFTR with an equalised-odds adversary on a comorbidity-risk task, with patients aged 70 or over as the protected group, then measures error-rate gaps for classifiers trained on held-out condition-prediction tasks, because fairness on those new tasks has to be measured rather than assumed.

A hospital imaging research group compares LAFTR with standard training for a chest X-ray triage classifier, with patient sex as the protected attribute and the model-selection rule fixed in advance, to decide whether debiasing the representation narrows the gap in error rates enough to justify its extra training cost.

limitations.description: The fairness bound holds only for an optimal adversary. A weak or under-trained adversary underestimates how much protected information the representation still carries, so downstream models can be less fair than training suggested; the authors report uneven results in places, which they attribute to unstable adversarial training. Audit downstream models directly, including with a fresh classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation.

Transfer to new tasks is not guaranteed for the error-rate criteria. The equalised-odds and equal-opportunity adversaries use the original task's labels, so fairness on a new task with different labels is an empirical result: in the paper's health-data experiment LAFTR was the fairest method on seven of ten transfer tasks, and the authors leave open which tasks transfer fairly.

As formulated, it handles one binary protected attribute and a binary task label; intersectional groups, several attributes or multi-class outcomes need an extension. Training needs the protected attribute and, for the error-rate criteria, the task labels. In the paper's experiments the encoder also took the protected attribute as input, so it is needed whenever new records are encoded; no results are reported without it.

Measured gains can be small in practice. MEDFAIR, a peer-reviewed benchmark of eleven bias-mitigation methods including LAFTR on medical imaging datasets, found the methods did not significantly improve fairness over standard training when trained and tested on the same task, including across datasets (it did not test transfer to new tasks), and that the model-selection criterion changed fairness results substantially. Compare against a standard model under a selection rule stated in advance.

Up to four networks (encoder, decoder, classifier, adversary) are trained against each other, with three weights balancing accuracy, reconstruction and fairness. The paper argues reconstruction is needed for transfer and used different weights for fair classification (accuracy 1, reconstruction 0) and for transfer (accuracy 0, reconstruction 1), so settings do not carry over. The 2018 reference code pins Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.9; reimplementations sit inside research benchmarks.

resources.title: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
resources.abstract: In this paper, we advocate for representation learning as the key to mitigating unfair prediction outcomes downstream. Motivated by a scenario where learned representations are used by third parties with unknown objectives, we propose and explore adversarial representation learning as a natural method of ensuring those parties act fairly. We connect group fairness (demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity) to different adversarial objectives. Through worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation, we show that the choice of this objective is crucial to fair prediction. Furthermore, we present the first in-depth experimental demonstration of fair transfer learning and demonstrate empirically that our learned representations admit fair predictions on new tasks while maintaining utility, an essential goal of fair representation learning.

resources.title: MEDFAIR: Benchmarking Fairness for Medical Imaging
resources.abstract: A multitude of work has shown that machine learning-based medical diagnosis systems can be biased against certain subgroups of people. This has motivated a growing number of bias mitigation algorithms that aim to address fairness issues in machine learning. However, it is difficult to compare their effectiveness in medical imaging for two reasons. First, there is little consensus on the criteria to assess fairness. Second, existing bias mitigation algorithms are developed under different settings, e.g., datasets, model selection strategies, backbones, and fairness metrics, making a direct comparison and evaluation based on existing results impossible. In this work, we introduce MEDFAIR, a framework to benchmark the fairness of machine learning models for medical imaging. MEDFAIR covers eleven algorithms from various categories, nine datasets from different imaging modalities, and three model selection criteria. Through extensive experiments, we find that the under-studied issue of model selection criterion can have a significant impact on fairness outcomes; while in contrast, state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms do not significantly improve fairness outcomes over empirical risk minimization (ERM) in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. We evaluate fairness from various perspectives and make recommendations for different medical application scenarios that require different ethical principles. Our framework provides a reproducible and easy-to-use entry point for the development and evaluation of future bias mitigation algorithms in deep learning. Code is available at https://github.com/ys-zong/MEDFAIR.

sample_claims.text: Classifiers trained by external parties on the released representation show a demographic parity difference below the agreed threshold on every downstream task audited.

A classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation released under the demographic parity objective does no better than always predicting the majority group, within an agreed margin.
The fairness of downstream risk models built on the shared encoded data was measured on each new prediction task rather than assumed from the task the encoder was trained on.
Under a model-selection rule fixed in advance, the debiased imaging model narrows the gap in error rates between patient groups relative to standard training by a measured margin.

techniques.name: Data Poisoning Detection
techniques.description: Data poisoning detection looks for training examples that an attacker has planted to change how a model behaves. The best-studied case is the backdoor: a few examples carrying a hidden trigger, such as a sticker on a stop sign, are mislabelled so that the model misclassifies any input with the trigger while it performs normally on clean data. Detection first trains a model on the untrusted data, then examines how that model represents each training example internally (its activations in the last hidden layer), one class at a time. Activation clustering splits a class into two groups by those activations and flags the smaller group when the split is clear, and spectral signatures score each example by its position along the main direction of variation and flag the highest scores. The flagged examples are reviewed or removed and the model is retrained, which yields a list of suspected examples and a measure of how cleanly each class separates.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a traffic-sign classifier for a driver-assistance system trains a trial model on images gathered from several suppliers and runs activation clustering on each class. A small separate group of stop-sign images labelled as speed limits, all carrying the same sticker, is flagged and removed before the final training run.

A research platform builds a chest X-ray classifier from images contributed by many partner hospitals. Before any partner's images enter the training set, it trains a trial model and scores each class for the small, separable group of examples a planted backdoor leaves, because one contributor's data could be compromised.

A platform trains a harmful-content classifier on labels supplied by crowd workers. Analysts scan each class for a small separate group of examples sharing a trigger phrase and labelled as harmless, which would let that phrase slip past the filter, and remove them before retraining.

An insurer trains a damage-assessment classifier on claims photos labelled by an outside vendor. Before relying on the labels, it scores each class for a small, separate group of photos carrying the same mark and labelled undamaged, which a compromised vendor account could have planted so that damaged vehicles with the mark pass unchecked. Flagged photos go back to the vendor for explanation.

limitations.description: An attacker who knows the detector can adapt. Both methods rely on poisoned examples standing out in the model's learned representation, so an attack that keeps them close to genuine examples can slip through. Chen et al. found no obvious way round activation clustering within their threat model, but say further work is needed.

False alarms can remove legitimate but unusual examples, reducing data quality and diversity. Chen et al. suggest a silhouette-score cut-off of about 0.10 to 0.15 based on three datasets; another data type or model may need different values, and a wrong value either removes good data or leaves poison in.

Both methods assume poisoned examples are a minority that separates from clean ones in the learned representation, and Tran et al.'s needs an upper bound on how many there are. They were designed and tested on backdoors in image and text classifiers, so attacks that only lower overall accuracy lie outside what the original papers show.

Both methods first train a model on the untrusted data, read its internal activations, then retrain after removing flagged examples. They need the full training data and white-box access to the model, and cost at least two training runs, so they cannot be applied to a model someone else trained when the data or weights are unavailable.

Real poison is unlabelled, so a detector's accuracy can only be measured on poison the tester injects, and a clean result shows that this detector found nothing, not that the data is clean. Telling poison from naturally unusual data is hard.

resources.title: Detecting Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks by Activation Clustering
resources.abstract: While machine learning (ML) models are being increasingly trusted to make decisions in different and varying areas, the safety of systems using such models has become an increasing concern. In particular, ML models are often trained on data from potentially untrustworthy sources, providing adversaries with the opportunity to manipulate them by inserting carefully crafted samples into the training set. Recent work has shown that this type of attack, called a poisoning attack, allows adversaries to insert backdoors or trojans into the model, enabling malicious behavior with simple external backdoor triggers at inference time and only a blackbox perspective of the model itself. Detecting this type of attack is challenging because the unexpected behavior occurs only when a backdoor trigger, which is known only to the adversary, is present. Model users, either direct users of training data or users of pre-trained model from a catalog, may not guarantee the safe operation of their ML-based system. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to backdoor detection and removal for neural networks. Through extensive experimental results, we demonstrate its effectiveness for neural networks classifying text and images. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first methodology capable of detecting poisonous data crafted to insert backdoors and repairing the model that does not require a verified and trusted dataset.

resources.title: Spectral Signatures in Backdoor Attacks
resources.abstract: A recent line of work has uncovered a new form of data poisoning: so-called \emph{backdoor} attacks. These attacks are particularly dangerous because they do not affect a network's behavior on typical, benign data. Rather, the network only deviates from its expected output when triggered by a perturbation planted by an adversary. In this paper, we identify a new property of all known backdoor attacks, which we call \emph{spectral signatures}. This property allows us to utilize tools from robust statistics to thwart the attacks. We demonstrate the efficacy of these signatures in detecting and removing poisoned examples on real image sets and state of the art neural network architectures. We believe that understanding spectral signatures is a crucial first step towards designing ML systems secure against such backdoor attacks

resources.title: SAFELOC: Overcoming Data Poisoning Attacks in Heterogeneous Federated Machine Learning for Indoor Localization
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) based indoor localization solutions are critical for many emerging applications, yet their efficacy is often compromised by hardware/software variations across mobile devices (i.e., device heterogeneity) and the threat of ML data poisoning attacks. Conventional methods aimed at countering these challenges show limited resilience to the uncertainties created by these phenomena. In response, in this paper, we introduce SAFELOC, a novel framework that not only minimizes localization errors under these challenging conditions but also ensures model compactness for efficient mobile device deployment. Our framework targets a distributed and co-operative learning environment that uses federated learning (FL) to preserve user data privacy and assumes heterogeneous mobile devices carried by users (just like in most real-world scenarios). Within this heterogeneous FL context, SAFELOC introduces a novel fused neural network architecture that performs data poisoning detection and localization, with a low model footprint. Additionally, a dynamic saliency map-based aggregation strategy is designed to adapt based on the severity of the detected data poisoning scenario. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that SAFELOC achieves improvements of up to 5.9x in mean localization error, 7.8x in worst-case localization error, and a 2.1x reduction in model inference latency compared to state-of-the-art indoor localization frameworks, across diverse building floorplans, mobile devices, and ML data poisoning attack scenarios.

resources.title: Zero-Shot Detection and Sanitization of Data Poisoning Attacks in Wearable AI Using Large Language Models
resources.abstract: Wearable AI systems, particularly in Human Activity Recognition (HAR), are becoming integral to applications in healthcare, security, and personal fitness due to the widespread adoption of smart devices and wearable technologies. However, the increasing reliance on machine learning models in HAR introduces significant risks, especially from poisoning attacks that compromise system reliability and data integrity. This paper explores the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect and sanitize poisoning attacks in wearable AI systems. Building on ongoing research into integrating LLMs within cyber-physical systems, we focus on sensor-based interactions with the physical world. Our case study seeks to answer the following question: How effective are LLMs in detecting and sanitizing poisoning attacks on human activity sensor data? Through zero-shot learning, we evaluate the performance of models such as ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4, and Gemini, providing insights into the viability of LLMs for real-time defense and data integrity in wearable AI systems.

techniques.name: Attacker-Model Re-identification Risk Measurement
techniques.description: Attacker-model re-identification risk measurement estimates, for a table of real records about people that is about to be released or shared, the probability that an attacker who links it with other information could correctly match a record to the person it describes. This record follows the attacker models of El Emam and Dankar (prosecutor and journalist) and of Dankar and El Emam (marketer), as implemented in the ARX tool: the assessor lists the quasi-identifiers (columns such as age, sex, postcode and admission date that an attacker could know or find), groups the records that share the same values on them, and names the attacker being guarded against. For a prosecutor, who knows the target is in the table, a record's risk is one over the size of its group in the table; for a journalist, who does not know this and links to a register of the wider population, it is one over the size of the matching group in that population, estimated with a statistical model when the population counts are not known; for a marketer, who tries to match as many records as possible, the measure is the expected share of records matched correctly. The assessor reports the highest record risk, the average risk and the share of records above a threshold set for the release, which decides whether the table can go out as it is or needs more generalisation or suppression first. It measures how easily records can be matched to people under the stated assumptions, unlike k-anonymity, which transforms the data, and it does not measure what can be learned about someone from values their whole group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A health insurer releasing claims data for a public prediction competition assumes an attacker who knows a neighbour's age, sex and a few of their claims, and measures each record's risk as one over the size of its group among all the insurer's members. It generalises ages and procedure codes until the measured probability of re-identification is below the 0.05 threshold agreed for the release, then checks the result with simulated matching attacks.

A pharmaceutical company sharing participant-level data from a completed trial with external researchers measures risk against the wider population, not the trial sample, because the participants are a small sample of everyone with the condition. It estimates how many records are unique in that population with ARX's uniqueness models and records the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, estimator and threshold in the data-sharing agreement for the researchers' data access committee to review.

A city transport authority planning to give a commuting dataset of home district, work district, age band and usual travel times to a contractor training a demand-forecasting model runs the assessment, finds a large share of records unique on home and work district together, merges small districts before sharing, and re-runs the assessment to confirm that the share of records above its threshold has fallen below the agreed limit.

limitations.description: The numbers are only as good as the list of quasi-identifiers and the attacker model behind them. A column left off the list, or an attacker who knows more (several of a person's hospital visits rather than one), can make records far easier to match than the assessment reports, and the assessor has to guess what other data an attacker holds. Repeating the assessment for stronger attackers, as some releases do with simulated matching, shows how sensitive the result is to these guesses.

It measures the chance of finding which record is a person's, not what can be learned about them. If all 20 records in a group share the same diagnosis, each has a measured risk of 1 in 20, yet anyone known to belong to the group has their diagnosis disclosed. Checks on the sensitive values, such as l-diversity, are needed alongside it when the release contains sensitive columns.

The journalist measure needs to know how common each record's values are in the wider population, which is rarely known and is estimated from the sample with statistical models; an evaluation of four estimators of population uniqueness on six clinical datasets found none accurate in all conditions. A small sample does not make re-identification unlikely in itself: one study estimated that 15 demographic attributes would let 99.98 per cent of Americans be correctly re-identified in any dataset.

There is no universal threshold, and the measure chosen changes the answer. For the same records the prosecutor measure is always at least as high as the journalist measure, so applying it to a release that is a small sample of a population over-protects and strips detail the data's users need; El Emam and Dankar found this effect strongest at small sampling fractions. The threshold, and which measure it applies to, must be justified for each release.

It measures one table as released, at one time. An attacker can combine several releases of the same data, or successive versions of a table that is updated, and longitudinal data, where each person has many events, need the attacker's knowledge of several events to be modelled explicitly. The basic measures do neither, so each additional or updated release needs its own assessment that takes the earlier ones into account.

techniques.name: k-Anonymity
techniques.description: k-Anonymity is a property that a table of real records about people can be made to satisfy before it is released or shared, in which every record shares its values on the quasi-identifiers with at least k-1 other records, so anyone linking the table to another source on those columns always matches a group of at least k records, which is k people only when each person has one record. Quasi-identifiers are columns that are not names or ID numbers but could be found elsewhere and combined to single a person out, such as date of birth, sex and postcode, and because the data holder chooses them, the protection covers only those columns. To reach a chosen k, each quasi-identifier is coarsened along a hierarchy set in advance (exact age to five-year band, full postcode to district), and the values or records that would still sit in a group smaller than k are suppressed, with a search choosing the coarsening that loses least information. The output is the transformed table of real records made less specific, not artificial ones, together with the k it achieves and a measure of the detail lost. Unlike differential privacy, it gives no bound on what an observer can learn, because it blocks linking on the listed columns but does not stop someone learning a sensitive value that everyone in a group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust preparing an extract of emergency attendances for a university research team treats age, sex, postcode district and attendance date as quasi-identifiers, since local news reports and social media posts about incidents often carry them. Using ARX it generalises age to five-year bands and dates to weeks, suppresses the records still in groups smaller than five, and sends the extract with a note of the k achieved, the columns covered and the share of records suppressed.

A national statistics office preparing a scientific-use file of a household survey for registered researchers recodes region and occupation into broader groups in sdcMicro, then applies local suppression until every combination of age band, sex, region and household size occurs at least three times, and publishes the number of suppressed values with the file so that users can judge the effect on their analyses.

A motor insurer sharing a claims table with an analytics firm that will build a fraud-detection model applies 10-anonymity to policyholder age, vehicle model and postcode district. Before release it agrees with the firm that the coarser bands still carry enough signal for the model, and it keeps the generalisation scheme so that later releases are generalised from the same scheme rather than a new one.

limitations.description: k-Anonymity hides which record is a person's, not what their group has in common. If all k records in a group share the same diagnosis, anyone who can place a person in that group learns the diagnosis, and an attacker with extra background knowledge can rule out other members of the group. Extensions such as l-diversity and t-closeness add conditions on the sensitive column for this reason; k-anonymity alone does not prevent sensitive values being disclosed.

The protection covers only the columns the data holder lists as quasi-identifiers, and rests on the holder judging correctly which columns an attacker could find elsewhere. A column left off the list, such as a rare diagnosis that a local newspaper has reported, can still single a record out, and the property says nothing about it. Choosing the list needs a realistic picture of the public, commercial and leaked data an attacker could hold.

Each release is protected only on its own. Two k-anonymous versions of the same data, generalised differently or produced at different times as records are added, can be joined to narrow groups below k, and two releases that keep the rows in the same order can be lined up row by row. Later releases must be built from the first, or treat all its released columns as quasi-identifiers, and row order must be randomised before each release.

With many quasi-identifiers or detailed values such as exact dates and measurements, most records are unique, and reaching k needs coarsening or suppression heavy enough to remove the detail an analysis or model depends on; the method suits continuous variables poorly. Because the suppressed records are those with rare combinations of values, the released table can under-represent exactly the unusual cases a model most needs to handle.

Requiring k within the released table treats the attacker as knowing their target is in it. When the table is a small sample of a larger population, a record unique in the table may match many people outside it, so the requirement over-protects; El Emam and Dankar found this over-anonymisation, and the loss of information it causes, greatest at small sampling fractions. A re-identification risk assessment against the population can justify a lighter transformation.

techniques.name: PII Detection and Redaction in Training Text
techniques.description: PII detection and redaction finds personally identifiable information (PII), such as names, email addresses, phone numbers and account or ID numbers, in a body of text and removes or replaces it before the text is used to train or fine-tune a model, so that the model has fewer personal details to memorise and later reproduce. Presidio, a widely used open-source tool first released by Microsoft and now run as an independent community project, is the reference implementation: each document passes through a set of recognisers, in which a named-entity recognition model (by default an English spaCy model) tags names, places and dates, patterns with checksum or format checks catch structured identifiers such as card and NHS numbers, and nearby words such as 'account' raise a candidate's confidence score. Every detection above a chosen score is then replaced with a placeholder for its type (for example <PERSON>), masked, hashed, encrypted or deleted, and the cleaned corpus goes to training. Because detection is never complete, the procedure ends by measuring recall, the share of identifiers actually caught, for each type on a hand-labelled sample of the same corpus. The evidence it produces is that measured miss rate and the cleaned corpus; unlike differential privacy or synthetic data, it removes real personal details from real text and gives no bound on what remains.

example_use_cases.description: A bank preparing two years of customer-service chat transcripts to fine-tune an assistant runs Presidio with added pattern recognisers for sort codes and its own account-number format, replaces each detection with a type placeholder, and has staff label 500 transcripts by hand to measure recall per entity type. It fine-tunes only once recall for names and account numbers meets the target in its data protection impact assessment, where it records the miss rate.

An NHS trust preparing discharge letters to fine-tune a summarisation model finds on a labelled sample that the default English model misses many names written in clinical shorthand and does not detect ward and bed codes at all. It adds lists of staff names and patterns for local codes, re-measures recall on a fresh labelled sample, and reports the remaining miss rate to its information governance group, which decides whether further controls are needed.

A company building a code-completion model from its internal repositories detects email addresses, IP addresses, keys and passwords with patterns and a trained detector, discards detections that are too short or are private network addresses to cut false alarms, replaces the rest with tokens such as <EMAIL> and <KEY>, and reports precision and recall per type on an annotated set of files kept apart from tuning.

limitations.description: Detection always misses some identifiers, and a model can memorise and reproduce what is missed, especially details repeated across many documents. A study that fine-tuned GPT-2 on court judgments and emails scrubbed with Presidio's default tagger and a second recogniser concluded that scrubbing reduces but cannot fully prevent leakage of personal information; Presidio's README gives no guarantee of finding it all. The evidence is a measured miss rate, not proof that none remains.

It finds only the categories it has recognisers for. On a 2022 benchmark of European Court of Human Rights judgments, Presidio's default setup caught about 70 per cent of identifying mentions but only about 45 per cent of direct identifiers, because it did not recognise case numbers, which identify the applicant on their own. Details that identify someone only in combination, such as a job title, employer and town, are not entity types at all, so redacted text can still point to a person.

The default recognisers are built for general English text. Clinical shorthand, other languages, source code and in-house identifier formats need extra recognisers or a different model, and recall measured on one corpus does not carry over to another, so the labelled sample used for the measurement must come from the corpus being cleaned and be kept apart from any tuning of the recognisers.

Raising recall by lowering the score threshold or switching on broad entity types also removes text that is not personal, such as names of public bodies, laws and places the task depends on, which lowers the value of the data for training. On the court-judgment benchmark, switching on organisation names raised Presidio's recall slightly but cut its precision from about 0.76 to 0.54.

Redaction removes identifiers from the text but does not hide whether a document was used for training, and it gives no formal bound. In the GPT-2 study, membership inference on the scrubbed model still reached an AUC of 0.82, where 0.5 is chance, and adding differentially private training brought it down to 0.5. Claims about membership, or a formal guarantee, need DP-SGD or another method alongside redaction.

techniques.name: Data Validation Checks
techniques.description: Data validation checks apply a written set of rules about what valid data look like to every new batch of data before a model is trained on it or uses it to make predictions, and flag or hold back any batch that breaks them. In Great Expectations (GX Core), a widely used open-source library for this, each rule is an expectation, a declarative assertion such as that a column exists and has a given type, has no missing values or takes values only from an allowed set or within a range (rules on single values can allow a stated share of rows to fail), or keeps a summary statistic (its mean, a quantile, or the divergence of its histogram from one built on reference data) within bounds the team sets. Expectations are grouped into a suite that a checkpoint runs on each batch as it arrives; the result records for every rule whether it passed and how many values broke it, with examples, configured actions can alert the team or update a human-readable report, and the pipeline can be set to stop training or scoring on a batch that failed. Running the same suite on training batches and on the data a deployed model receives catches differences between the two, such as a feature that is always missing in production, before they degrade predictions; unlike out-of-distribution detectors, the checks need no model and judge whole batches against explicit rules rather than scoring single inputs, and unlike runtime monitoring of a deployed model they act before the model sees the data. Unlike a kernel two-sample test, its distribution rules are fixed bounds set by the team, not a statistical test of whether two samples differ.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider feeds surveillance track reports into a model that predicts aircraft arrival times. Its data engineers run an expectation suite on every incoming batch, covering required fields, units, plausible ranges for altitude and ground speed, and the share of reports with missing positions, so that a sensor change that silently switched altitude from feet to metres would stop the batch before it reached the model rather than surface weeks later as worse predictions.

A weather service that retrains a statistical correction model each month on station observations validates every monthly extract first: station identifiers must come from the station list, temperatures must lie within each station's climatological limits, no variable may have more than 2 per cent missing values, and each variable's mean and quantiles must stay within bounds set from earlier years. A failed check stops the retraining and opens a ticket listing the failing stations.

A hospital running a deterioration-risk model on laboratory results checks each hourly batch from the laboratory system against expectations for test codes, units and value ranges, so that if a laboratory changes the unit of a test without notice the batch is flagged and risk scores for the affected patients are withheld until the mapping is corrected.

A bank's credit-scoring team runs the expectation suite written for its training data on a daily sample of the applications its deployed model scores and compares the results, so that a field the online form has stopped collecting, which the scoring service quietly fills with a default value, shows up as a difference between training and production data rather than as an unexplained drop in approval rates.

limitations.description: Checks catch only what someone thought to write down. A batch can satisfy every rule and still be wrong in a way no rule covers, such as a changed relationship between two columns or a change in how labels were assigned. GX Core does not infer rules from the data, since its automatic profilers were removed in version 1.0, so each rule has to be specified, and for pipelines with thousands of features that effort can put teams off setting up validation at all.

Bounds for distribution rules are hard to set. Statistical tests on large batches fire on differences too small to matter: in Google's data validation paper, a chi-square test between 100 million points and a copy with 0.01 per cent of them redrawn from a wider distribution raised an alert in 7 of 10 trials, while thresholds on divergence measures such as KL divergence are hard for teams to interpret. Bounds are therefore tuned by trial, risking too many alerts or missed shifts.

The rules describe the input data, not the model's performance. A batch that passes can still produce wrong predictions if the relationship between inputs and outcomes has changed (concept drift), and a batch that fails shows that the data changed, not that predictions got worse, so the checks need pairing with monitoring of performance once outcomes arrive.

Alerts help only if someone acts on them, and rules need upkeep as data legitimately change. In Google's deployment across more than 700 pipelines, new columns, unexpected values and missing columns were the commonest anomalies, most pipelines revised their schema, and between 28 and 100 per cent of fired anomalies of each kind were fixed, which the authors attribute partly to operators missing or ignoring alerts.

The checks work on tables: GX Core connects to data frames, SQL databases and data files, so for images, audio, free text or gridded weather fields the team must first compute a table of properties, such as sizes, value ranges or missing tiles, and write rules about those. This catches broken or truncated inputs but not changes in what the content shows.
